messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content:
I'm making a bot that's supposed to be able to at least partially function as a RPG in the vein of LitRPGs (a genre of novels and light novels with game-like mechanics such as classes, character sheets, etc), and I have a few questions if anyone else has tried something similar while using a lorebook for rules and worldbuilding.

First, let's say it's a D&D game (it's not), let's say I mention Classes in the description, I presume that will make the bot look up the Classes Lorebook entry, seeing it's a list of Fighter, Barbarian, Sorcerer etc. so it can offer an appropriate class to user, likewise if during the roleplay an enemy Sorcerer becomes involved, the bot will be able to reference the Sorcerer lorebook entry (or be referred there from the Classes entry) and find how a Sorcerer functions? Please clarify if any of this is wrong.

Secondly, say I want combat (using D&D 3e for the reference since it's what I'm most familiar with, again it's not going to be that in the actual thing), can I have a Combat lorebook entry that the bot will reference to be able to adjudicate it, so it looks up hit points, armor class, saving throws, the sorcerer spell that just hit me, etc? 

Or will the bot most likely be extremely confused by all these details and start hallucinating, and it's better to KISS and be good with it just making shit up most of the time, instead providing it examples how it should go?

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
The harsh reality is this... the MORE COMPLEX the bot is, the more likely it will hallucinate shit.

In order to avoid hallucinations, the important information needs to remain consistent and update every message.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content: For example, if you want a stats system, it would need to display at the top of every message

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: sigh, yeah I was afraid of that, KISS and let it make up shit is probably better. every LITRPG novel has their own rules and shit anyway

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: I was thinking something like making sure that your stats are always in a sticky message in the memories

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content: Its easy to code, but it will limit the dialogue and action text the more stuff you need to track

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: yeah I'm not trying to make a wargame, in LitRPGs the stats and stuff tends to be just primarily background elements, justifications not unlike superhero books and similar really

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: so, KISS it is, and paintstakingly implementing my homebrew system is probably just a waste of time, lol, thanks Josh.

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: (And for the record, I'm still unsubbed, I'm just on a yearly sub that expires in Oct lol, so I figured I'd try SFW shit since NSFW is always getting interfered with due to those darn rules)

messages.author: Lyfiã
messages.content: Hey <@216685487459532800>, are you still considering this idea? I haven't tested this exact LitRPG setup myself, so I don't want to overpromise, but I think there may be a workable way to structure it using a mix of Scenario rules, a story-specific Lorebook, and a small current-stats/state entry. If you're still interested, I can explain what I have in mind.

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: I tried it and I implemented all of the rules, but the bot will ignore the rules half of the time, I had 19 entries in my lore book to cover the various standard things from LitRPG settings (stats, skills, monsters, magic, loot, dungeons, towers, etc). It works half of the time at least?

messages.author: Lyfiã
messages.content: <@216685487459532800> Oh, you actually tested it quite extensively then 😄 19 Lorebook entries is much more than I assumed from the older conversation. When you say it ignored the rules half of the time, do you remember how you handled the triggers and the current stats/state? I’m wondering whether the problem was partly that the relevant rule entries weren’t always in context. The way I structure Lorebooks now, I’d probably keep the core system rules in Scenario, use a frequently triggered entry for the rules/current state that always need to be available, and only trigger things like individual classes, monsters or skills when they’re relevant.

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content:
I did a few play tests, my first character everything worked out okay, my character started normal, did his first thing and got his class, and it everything seemed to work as it would, even if it played very fast and lose with combat rules. For the second character (very different persona) there was even faster and looser combat, followed by a custom class suited to that character, except the AI kept the character sheet, but completely made up how magic worked and how much my spells cost, and because it kept only parts of the rules the result was a very useless character.

I was going to rewrite it to try to cut it down to as simple as possible so the bot can just make up the system and details, but I haven't gotten around to it because of how much work it was to set up the first one.

messages.author: Lyfiã
messages.content:
That actually makes me think the idea may be more salvageable than it first sounded. I haven't tested this exact LitRPG setup myself, so I don't want to promise it would solve everything, but I use Lorebooks quite heavily for long-term RP now and I'd probably structure it a little differently.
I wouldn't rely on all 19 entries equally. I'd keep only the absolute system rules in Scenario — things like established stats/costs being canon, resources having to be deducted consistently, and the current character state taking priority over improvisation.
Then I'd use the Lorebook for the detailed class, magic, monster, skill, loot etc. rules, with very deliberate triggers. For the rules/state that need to be available almost constantly, I'd use a very common trigger so the entry behaves almost like an always-on memory.
The biggest thing I'd change based on what happened with your second character is keeping a short Current Stats / Current Build entry. Not just HP/MP, but the character's currently known skills/spells and their fixed costs. If the AI creates a custom class, I'd also “freeze” its core rules there once it's created, otherwise those details can eventually drift out of context and get reinvented.
I'd probably also give it one concrete combat example in the Greeting or Example Dialogue and then use the same format consistently myself.
It still wouldn't be a perfect game engine, especially for complicated arithmetic, but since your first test actually worked, I wonder if simplifying the rules that must always be present rather than simplifying the whole system might get you further.

messages.author: Sacremas
messages.content: Thanks for the suggestions, and yeah relying more on elements of the description and scenario over lore books was something I was going to try, I've just not gotten around to it. I'll mess around with it a bit more, but I also want to try to just simplify the whole thing down and see how much the AI actually understands the LitRPG concept without pushing too many details. If it's going to make up stuff, I might as well give it free reign to try to figure out something interesting each time after all. For instance I might have the scenario tell it to give the user an appropriate character sheet with vital stats, rather than specifically spelling out the actual stats of my homebrew simple RPG system for it to use.

messages.author: Lyfiã
messages.content:
Yeah, I actually think that could work better if your goal is more narrative LitRPG than simulating a strict RPG system. If the AI is going to invent parts of the system anyway, deliberately giving it room to do that might produce much more interesting results than trying to force every stat and mechanic.
The one thing I'd probably still define is what happens after it invents something. Something like: once a class, stat, ability, resource or cost has been established in the story, it becomes part of that character's continuity and shouldn't randomly change unless progression or an event changes it.
So you could let it invent an appropriate character sheet rather than specifying your whole homebrew system, while still giving it a basic consistency rule. I'd actually be curious how well that works in testing.
